input: A centuries old vampire gets really into video games because playing a character who can walk around in the sun is the closest thing they have to experiencing the day again in centuries.
output:
The sunlight on the screen was the color of honey. 

Lysander’s fingers twitched against the controller, guiding his in-game avatar—a broad-shouldered farmhand with a laugh that gusted like summer wind—through a wheat field. Pixelated gold rippled under a digital sky so blue it ached. He’d forgotten that blue. Forgotten the way heat could pool in the hollow of a collarbone, or how dust motes danced in slanting daylight. Three hundred years since he’d seen it firsthand. Three centuries of shadows, of cramped rooms reeking of mothballs and blackout curtains. 

But here, in *Stardawn Valley*, he could pretend. 

The farmhand knelt to plant tulip bulbs. Lysander’s throat tightened. He remembered doing that once, in another life. His human hands caked with soil, sweat trickling down his neck as his sister teased him for fussing over “fragile little things.” The memory was frayed, eroded by time, but the game’s idle soundtrack—soft guitar strings, a humming chorus—stitched the fragments together. 

A notification blinked: *SunnyGurl92 wants to join your session!* 

He hesitated. Multiplayer was risky. But loneliness, he’d found, was sharper than sunlight. He hit *Accept*. 

“Dude, your farm is *epic*,” came a voice through the headset, bright and crackling with static. “How’d you get the sunflowers so big?” 

Lysander smiled. “Blood sacrifice.” 

SunnyGurl92’s avatar—a pink-haired chef in overalls—snort-laughed. “Hardcore. I just use fertilizer.” They spent the next hour trading seeds and bad jokes. She didn’t ask why he only played at night. He didn’t ask about the tremor in her hands when she mentioned her “offline” job at a hospice. The game’s perpetual noon stretched on, forgiving. 

At 4:57 a.m., Lysander’s skin began to prickle. Dawn lurked beyond the apartment’s sealed windows. “I have to go,” he said abruptly. 

“Wait! Let’s visit the mountain summit first. The sunrise there is insane.” 

His cursor hovered over *Exit Game*. Human cruelty was so mundane, so *accidental*. “...One minute.” 

They sprinted up the pixelated trail. The farmhand’s boots crunched pretend snow. At the peak, the screen softened into watercolor hues—pink, peach, amber. Lysander’s chest burned. He couldn’t tell if it was the vampire curse or grief. 

“Pretty, right?” SunnyGurl92 whispered. 

The first time he’d burned, age 24, he’d been chasing a stray lamb at dawn. There’d been no pain at first—just a brilliant white light, then centuries of darkness. Now, he stared at the simulated sunrise until his eyes stung. The farmhand lifted his pixel face to the sky, and Lysander let himself sway, just a little, imagining the warmth. 

He logged off as the in-game sun cleared the horizon. Outside, real daylight seeped through the curtains’ edges. Lysander retreated to his closet, laptop clutched to his chest. The farmhand’s laughter echoed in the dark, a secondhand ghost. 

He dreamed of tulips.

input: A psychic alien who feeds on dreams comes to Earth for the first time. Turns out humans are the only sentients in the galaxy that have nightmares.
output:
Zyrath’s tendrils trembled as they brushed the atmosphere, tasting the psychic residue of a billion sleeping minds. They had feasted across seven galaxies, sipping the pastel tranquility of dreams where sentients floated in serene, weightless joy. But Earth… Earth *reeked*. Its psychic aura coiled like smoke, acrid and jagged, laced with something Zyrath’s translator-cells struggled to name. Not fear. Not sorrow. Something that *burned*.  

The first nightmare hit as they phased through a suburban roof.  

A child’s scream. Teeth like shattered mirrors. A shadow with too many joints crawling up a wall. Zyrath recoiled, membranes stinging—until the aftertaste registered. Beneath the terror thrummed a metallic tang, rich and dark, vibrating with a depth no nectar-sweet dream had ever offered. They followed the thread downward.  

The woman thrashing in bed smelled of salt and unwashed hair. Clara, her mind hissed. Thirty-two revolutions around this yellow star. Five since the accident. The nightmare unfolded like rotting parchment: a minivan’s screech, a tiny shoe in rain-soaked asphalt, the ceaseless beep of a hospital monitor. Zyrath hesitated. To feed here felt profane, like drinking from an open wound.  

They drank anyway.  

It was a supernova in reverse—all that collapsing fury, that crushing weight of *what if* and *if only*. Zyrath’s bioluminescence flickered erratically as human neurochemicals flooded their system: cortisol sharp as broken glass, adrenaline like white-hot wires. They tried to pull away, but Clara’s psyche clung, desperate. Her grief wasn’t a static painting but a living thing, thrashing, *evolving*.  

By dawn, Zyrath huddled in her attic, quivering. They’d consumed rage that left phantom bruises, guilt that gnawed like stomach acid, shame sticky as blood. Yet when Clara woke, she breaked coffee, humming a fractured lullaby. She lived.  

The alien observed her for weeks. Humans, they realized, were creatures of paradox. They buried nightmares under daylight rituals—laughed with broken voices, kissed with trembling lips. Each night, Zyrath gorged, drunk on horrors that somehow *strengthened* these fragile beings. A soldier’s flashbacks carried the crispness of survival; a widow’s recurrent darkness pulsed with undimmed love.  

One midnight, Clara’s nightmare shifted. The hospital beep dissolved into a meadow. Her daughter’s laughter echoed from behind a birch tree, always just out of sight. “I know you’re not real,” Clara whispered in the dream, tears hot. “But stay.”  

Zyrath fed, and this time, the aftertaste was different. Bitter, yes, but beneath it, something like the first rain after wildfire.  

They never left Earth. The galaxy’s other species pitied humanity, these shrieking, bleeding dreamers. But Zyrath swam in their stormy seas, learning a truth no tranquil mind could grasp: nightmares were not poison. They were the price, the alchemy, the forge.  

When the next star-farer asked why Zyrath’s light now flickered charcoal and crimson, they answered:  

“You savor still waters. I found an ocean that burns.”

input: Aliens take over the Earth. They then announce that they will be forcing the humans to work a ‘tyrannical’ 4 hours a day 4 days a week in exchange for basic rights like housing. Needless to say they are very confused when the humans celebrate their new alien overlords
output:
The saucers descended on a Tuesday, obsidian and silent, blotting out the sun. When the Vorath emerged—tall, iridescent-skinned, their four eyes blinking in unison—they broadcast their demands in a voice like grinding stone. *“Your labor sustains us now. Four hours daily, four days weekly. Compliance grants shelter, sustenance, survival. Resistance is extinction.”*  
  
The crowd in Times Square gaped. Then someone laughed.  
  
It began as a stifled snort, then erupted into full-bodied howls. A woman hugged a stranger, tears streaking her face. “Four hours?” a man shouted, waving his phone. “I used to bill *twelve* for consulting!” The Vorath’s cranial ridges flushed crimson, a sign of agitation. Their High Overseer, Kl’ra, tilted her head, mandibles twitching. “Why do they… *rejoice*?” she asked her second, V’tik. “Our simulations predicted revolt.”  
  
The humans were already composing ballads. Memes of Vorath in party hats flooded TikTok. Unions demanded the aliens *formalize* the arrangement: “Make the four-hour day legally binding!”  
  
Kl’ra ordered a human brought aboard her ship—a midlevel marketing manager named Luis, still clutching a “THANK U, OVERLORDS!” latte. “Explain this… *gratitude*,” she demanded. Luis shrugged. “Before you came, I worked sixty-hour weeks. Couldn’t afford my apartment. My kid’s daycare cost half my salary.” He sipped his latte. “Now I garden. Teach her chess. You guys gave us *time*.”  
  
The Vorath exchanged glances. On their homeworld, productivity was sacred; citizens cycled through twenty-hour shifts, sustained by nutrient pastes, their worth measured in output. Leisure was decadence. Survival was earned through relentless toil.  
  
“You see this as *generosity*?” V’tik muttered.  
  
“We see it as not being exploited,” Luis said.  
  
Kl’ra’s exoskeleton paled. She’d intended to break them, to harvest their grit. Instead, she’d unearthed a fragility her algorithms hadn’t comprehended: a species so accustomed to being drained that a trickle felt like a flood.  
  
Later, watching humans picnicking in parks they’d once only hurried through, Kl’ra felt a pang of something alien. “Perhaps,” she mused to V’tik, “we underestimated their definition of tyranny.”  
  
“Or overestimated their tolerance for suffering,” V’tik replied.  
  
The Vorath recalibrated. They mandated “recreational intervals” and capped productivity metrics, baffled when humans used the extra hours to bake bread, write poetry, rebuild eroded communities. Resistance cells did form—not against the Vorath, but against attempts to revert to the old ways. “Keep your forty-hour hellscape!” graffiti read. “We’re thriving.”  
  
Kl’ra never admitted it, but she began lingering near Earth’s oceans at dusk, studying the way humans sat quietly, watching waves. Once, she downloaded a novel. *Ulysses*. She understood none of it, yet…  
  
“They’re *happy*,” she told V’tik.  
  
“A flaw?”  
  
“A revelation.”  
  
The Vorath’s conquest became a quiet revolution. Uprisings flickered on distant worlds when news spread: the humans, with their four-hour days, had somehow conquered *back*. Not through weapons, but by unshackling something in the Vorath’s own soul. Kl’ra’s reports grew poetic, then personal. She resigned her post, requested asylum.  
  
“I wish to learn,” she told Luis, “how to sit. How to… *be*.” He taught her to sip coffee slowly, to name the stars without mapping them. The galaxy’s most efficient overlords became its most reluctant philosophers, whispering a dangerous truth: maybe survival wasn’t everything. Maybe there was more.  
  
The saucers still hover, but now, they cast shadows that feel like shelter.

input: Humanity is visited by a cosmic horror the likes of which has only been seen in Lovecraftian horror. In desperation, Earth throws everything we have at it, and, miraculously, the human race has killed a God. Somewhere in a realm beyond our understanding, the other gods speak of the event.
output:
The sky wept ash the day we killed a god.  

They called it Xal’thar, a name scraped from static between radio telescopes. It arrived as a bruise on the horizon, a tumor of tentacles and eyes that drank starlight. Its voice was a bassline in our bones, promising dissolution. Armies shattered. Cities folded like origami into its maw. We were ants scuttling beneath a boot—until President Ruiz, her voice frayed on live TV, said, “Throw it all. *Everything*.”  

Nuclear arsenals. Hypersonic rails. AI-piloted drones sharp as razors. They dissolved like sugar in water. Dr. Elena Li, who’d once studied dementia, noticed the pattern: Xal’thar consumed *order*. Machinery. Algorithms. “It’s eating our *certainty*,” she whispered. Her hands shook as she proposed the alternative—a neural net, wired into every surviving human. A weapon of chaos. Of *dreams*.  

We huddled in bunkers, in subway tunnels, in forests singing with wildfires. Electrodes clung to our temples. “Think of grief,” Li urged. “Of love. Of the *mess*.” The system harvested it all—the man in Oslo cradling his dead dog, the girl in Mumbai humming a lullaby to her brother, the thousand million private hungers. We became a storm.  

Xal’thar recoiled. For the first time, its tentacles *twisted*, eyes dimming. It screamed in a frequency that burst dams, that crumbled limestone. But we screamed louder.  

When it died, the silence was a held breath.  

---  

Somewhere else, in a vault between entropy and time, the gods convened.  

“A *mortal* wound,” hissed Yg’nath, whose form was a calculus of spirals. Its voice dissolved into echoes: *mortal, mortal, mortal*.  

The assembly shuddered. Their shapes defied geometry—a nest of black veins, a sigh with teeth, a hunger that wore supernovas as jewelry.  

“They weaponized… *ambiguity*,” said The One Who Gnaws, tendrils flickering with disdain. “How?”  

Memories were exchanged, viscous and reluctant. A species that built cathedrals of questions. That named constellations after dead lovers. That clung to fragile meanings in a meaningless void.  

The Starving Maw, eldest of them, pulsed slowly. “We assumed their chaos made them weak. But it *bent*. It *folded*.” A pause, thick with unease. “Xal’thar’s essence is… *scattered*. They have tasted godhood.”  

A colder silence now.  

“Do they know?” whispered The Dread That Sings in Marrow.  

The Maw’s light dimmed. “They will.”  

---  

On Earth, survivors emerged, squinting at a sun that seemed too gentle. Li knelt in the ruins of Geneva, a neural node still glued to her wrist. Her toddler’s laughter looped in her head—a file she’d uploaded to the net. *Was that you, mi vida?*  

In the soil beneath her, something glistened. Not shrapnel. Not bone. A shard of *night*, vibrating softly. When she touched it, visions erupted: vast intelligences recoiling, a chorus of dread. *What are we now?*  

Above, satellites blinked. The nodes were still active. Still listening.  

Li smiled, dizzy.  

Somewhere, a god shuddered.

input: Instead of the Monkey’s Paw, you find the Clown’s Nose, which instead of granting your wish in the worst way possible will grant it in the funniest way.
output:
**The Clown’s Nose**  

Eleanor found it tucked between a taxidermied ferret and a ceramic unicorn in the back of Granny Mae’s Thrift Shoppe—a rubber clown nose, crimson and glossy, with a tag that read *“Laughter Guaranteed! (Or Your Soul Back!”)*. The cashier, a woman with mothball-scented hair, hissed, “Careful, dear. Last owner joined a cult. *Sober* one.” Eleanor, two months behind on rent and freshly dumped via Post-It, bought it for 50 cents.  

That night, she squeezed the nose. It honked.  

“I wish I had rent money,” she muttered.  

The ceiling exploded.  

Not with cash, but with rubber chickens. Dozens rained down, each squawking, *“CLUCK-A-DOODLE-DOO!”* Eleanor pried one open—a $20 bill fluttered out. Another—a roll of quarters. Another—a coupon for 10% off existential despair. By dawn, she’d harvested $1,200.37 and a newfound fear of poultry.  

“Funny,” she told the nose. “But *why chickens*?”  

It honked again.  

——  

Wish two: “I want someone to love me.”  

The doorbell rang. A mime stood there, striped shirt, tear painted on his cheek. He handed her a balloon poodle. When she laughed, he mimed a heart exploding. They shared wine—he pantomimed chugging, she actual-chugged. By midnight, they slow-danced to silent music, his hands shaping an invisible radio playing *Careless Whisper*. Eleanor’s ex had never serenaded her via imaginary saxophone.  

But when she woke, the mime was gone. In his place: a life-sized origami swan with “*MERCI*” inked on its wing. The nose, smug on her nightstand, honked.  

——  

“Undo it!” she yelled, clutching the nose. “I want my normal, *boring* life back!”  

Her apartment quaked. The walls peeled into striped tent fabric. Her couch sprouted popcorn. Her tabby, Mr. Whiskers, materialized in a tiny clown car, honking the horn with his paw. A call from her principal: “Eleanor, why is the schoolhouse *literally* a big top?”  

She stormed outside. Neighbors juggled hedgehogs. Fire hydrants sprayed confetti. A cop pulled her over for “excessive whimsy.”  

“Fix this!” she screamed at the nose.  

It honked.  

——  

Eleanor sat on a sidewalk, watching a pug skateboard in a tutu. The sun dipped, painting the chaos gold. She’d spent months aching for control—over bills, love, her crooked bangs. Now, the world was a punchline, and she… *wasn’t laughing*.  

She squeezed the nose. “Okay, fine. What’s the joke?”  

Silence. Then, a whisper: *“You.”*  

Eleanor blinked. Then snorted. Then cackled, wild and loud, until her ribs ached. The nose warmed in her hand, melting into goo. Around her, the circus faded. Tents became brick; confetti, leaves. Mr. Whiskers reappeared, licking his paw, unimpressed.  

On her desk, the nose—now ordinary rubber—sat beside a note: *“Laughter’s just fear, upside-down. – Marcel (The Mime)”*  

Eleanor pinned the nose to her coat. That Friday, she took her students to the park, taught geometry via hula-hoops. When rain drenched them, she honked the nose, and the puddles sprouted rainbows.  

The principal called it “unorthodox.”  

The kids called it magic.

input: A centuries old vampire gets really into video games because playing a character who can walk around in the sun is the closest thing they have to experiencing the day again in centuries.
output: Elias hadn’t touched daylight in 237 years. Not since the fever took his sister, and he’d stumbled into that crypt, half-delirious, bargaining with shadows. Now he lived in a studio above a Brooklyn bodega, the blinds sealed with duct tape. His skin smelled of old paper and the ozone crackle of CRT monitors.  The game was called Sunhaven Acres. A farming simulator. He’d bought it ironically, then become obsessed.  His avatar, Henry, wore overalls and a straw hat. Each morning, Henry stepped onto a pixelated porch, stretched, and yawned at a sunrise rendered in 8-bit gold. Elias would lean close, the monitor’s glow etching his gaunt face blue, and guide Henry through chores—tilling soil, milking cows, tossing feed to chickens that clucked in tinny MIDI. At noon, Henry napped under an oak tree while light dappled his overalls. Elias never skipped this part. He’d watch the screen until his eyes burned, imagining warmth on his neck.  “You’re always online,” messaged Marisol89, a fellow player. Her avatar wore a witch hat and sold enchanted turnips.  “Night owl,” Elias typed. His fingers hesitated. Night was too small a word.  The game’s nights were brief, just ten minutes of starry sky before dawn. Elias hated them. He’d send Henry to bed early, resetting the cycle. Once, Marisol89 asked why he never visited her night market. “Bad eyes,” he lied. “The dark strains them.”  When the shutdown notice came—Sunhaven Acres servers closing permanently June 1st—Elias drank three bags of O-negative and smashed his mug. Shards glittered like the chandeliers he’d known in Versailles. He logged on at 4:58 AM, one hour before server death.  Marisol89 was waiting by the virtual lake. “Last sunrise,” she said. Her avatar held a lantern.  Henry stood still as the horizon blushed. Elias’s hand hovered over the keyboard. Somewhere below, a garbage truck beeped. A drunk couple argued in Spanish. The city was waking up, and he would soon retreat to his coffin—a modified refrigerator lined with blackout curtains.  “Why the farming thing?” Marisol89 asked. “You never even grow crops.”  Elias made Henry kneel, a glitchy animation. The first sunbeam crested the hills. “Reminds me of my sister’s garden,” he typed. True, but incomplete. Clara had grown rosemary and lavender. She’d believed sunlight cured melancholy.  The server clock blinked 5:59. Elias leaned until his forehead touched the screen. The pixels blurred. For a moment, he could almost feel it—the way Clara used to grab his wrist, pulling him into meadows, her laugh bright and scolding. You’ll turn to stone, reading all day!  At 6:00 AM, the screen died. Error 404: Sunrise Not Found.  Downstairs, the bodega’s awning rattled up. Sunlight sliced the alley. Elias pressed a palm to the window’s edge, watching smoke curl from his seared skin. He’d done this every June 1st since 1983. A birthday ritual.  By dusk, the blisters would heal. He’d buy another game—Azure Skies, maybe, or Daybreak Chronicles. For now, he closed his eyes and let the pain ferment into memory. Clara’s garden. The way noon smelled when you weren’t afraid of it.  Somewhere, a child laughed. Elias bared his fangs at the empty room, tasting old blood and older longing. The monitor’s afterimage lingered behind his lids: a phantom sun, blue as a vein, fading.

input: A psychic alien who feeds on dreams comes to Earth for the first time. Turns out humans are the only sentients in the galaxy that have nightmares.
output: The first time it tastes a nightmare, the alien chokes.  It had expected pastel reveries, the sugary mists of Earth’s dreamscape. Instead, it gags on bile and smoke, on the coppery tang of phantom blood. Humans, it realizes, trembling behind the borrowed face of a gas station attendant, carry their hells inside them.  The alien’s species thrives on the soft hum of contentment—the dreams of a thousand placid civilizations, all pastel and predictable. But this... this is a symphony of teeth. A woman at Pump 3 clutches her coffee, her mind a battleground: her son’s crib empty again, his laughter curdling into sirens. The alien staggers, flooded by her grief. It’s alive. It’s alive in a way no dream has ever been.  By dawn, it’s addicted.  It finds her in the parking lot of a 24-hour diner. Marlene, 58, her hair still streaked with the burgundy of younger years. She dreams awake now—fingers drumming the steering wheel, eyes darting to rearview mirrors. The alien slips into the passenger seat, its form rippling like a mirage.  “Mind if I join?” it asks, though permission is irrelevant.  Marlene’s nightmare is a living thing: her brother’s Ford submerged in Lake Pontchartrain, his knuckles white on the wheel. She was twelve. She survived.  “You’re not real,” she mutters, knuckles matching her brother’s.  The alien feasts. Agony sears its throat, but beneath the rot, it finds something else—the frantic pulse of survival, the raw want to wake up. It’s grotesque. It’s exquisite.  Nights blur. The alien forgets to shed Marlene’s skin.  They drive. She talks in fragments: the way her brother’s voice cracks in her memory, the paramedic who called her “honey” as he wrapped her in foil. The alien’s hunger sharpens, but so does a nagging ache—a craving not for the nightmare, but for the woman who rebuilds herself inside it.  “Why stay?” it asks one night, the highway stretching endless.  Marlene grips the wheel. “Where else would I go?”  The alien hesitates. Reveals a sliver of truth: “My kind… we drift. We consume.”  “Yeah?” She laughs, brittle. “Welcome to the club.”  It happens in Oklahoma. Marlene dreams awake, the Ford’s headlights slicing through darkness. The alien reaches for the nightmare—and recoils.  It’s different.  The water isn’t freezing. The dashboard glows softly. Her brother turns, smiling. “You did good,” he says, though he never spoke again.  Marlene’s cheeks are wet. “Took me decades to let him say that.”  The alien trembles. This isn’t consumption; it’s communion.  When the craving returns, the alien hesitates. It could find fresher pain—a veteran’s flashback, a widow’s restless bed. But here, in this rusted Taurus, there’s a new flavor beneath the ash: not the absence of fear, but the choice to swallow it whole.  “Stay,” Marlene says, not looking over.  The alien peels off its borrowed faces. Lets her see the void beneath, the hunger etched into its core.  Marlene nods. “Yeah,” she whispers. “Me too.”  They drive east, the road humming beneath them. The alien learns to savor the aftertaste of nightmares—the stubborn, unyielding dawn that follows.

input: Aliens take over the Earth. They then announce that they will be forcing the humans to work a ‘tyrannical’ 4 hours a day 4 days a week in exchange for basic rights like housing. Needless to say they are very confused when the humans celebrate their new alien overlords
output:
The game was called Sunhaven Acres. A farming simulator. He’d bought it ironically, then become obsessed.The hologram flickered above Town Hall, casting an emerald sheen on faces upturned like sun-starved flowers. The Zyrathi’s voice buzzed through translation devices implanted in every throat: “Four solar cycles weekly. Four hours daily. Compliance ensures sustenance modules and domicile allocations.”

A beat of silence. Then, laughter rolled through the crowd—wet, jagged, disbelieving. Someone began clapping. Clara felt the sound in her molars, a childhood memory surfacing: her father’s calloused hands applauding her mother’s third consecutive night shift at the hospital.

“They think they’re punishing us,” whispered Mr. Park beside her. His fingernails still bore the grease stains of twelve-hour shifts at the shuttered auto plant.

On her first work assignment, Clara scrubbed biofilm from hexagonal towers while the Zyrathi supervisor, Gloam, hovered behind her. Her scrubber whirred against translucent walls, revealing dizzying views of the resurrected prairie below.

“Your pulse elevates,” Gloam intoned, eyestalks quivering. “Explain this physiological response to leisure intervals.”

Clara paused. The translation implant itched. “You’re giving us six hours back each day. Sir.”

“Correct. To demonstrate our dominance.”

She bit her lip, hiding a smile. The towers’ anti-microbial sheen felt nothing like the Dollar General’s sticky floors, where she’d once stocked shelves until 2 AM while Luna’s babysitter texted She’s asking when you’ll be real home.

That evening, Clara cooked actual garlic—a luxury when the Walmart closed—as Luna chattered about Gloam’s “playtime protocols” requiring guardians to spend 19:00-20:30 with offspring.

“Mrs. Nguyen says they’re brainwashing us,” Luna said, kneading cookie dough with hands already steadier than her mother’s.

Clara inhaled steam from boiling pasta, her skull throbbing with the phantom weight of a customer service headset. “Old Mrs. Nguyen worked 80 years without a pension. Let her call this brainwashing.”

Gloam intercepted Clara at the hydration station. “Your peer group exhibits counterintuitive dopamine spikes during mandatory community gardens.”

Clara sipped her rationed electrolyte fluid, now uncontaminated with microplastics. “You ever see someone try to grow tomatoes in a meth lab parking lot?”

The alien’s bioluminescent stripes pulsed orange—the manual said this signaled profound confusion. Clara pocketed an extra seed packet, still marveling at vegetables that didn’t glow.

At the solstice reconditioning ceremony, Gloam presented Clara with a “model worker” medal. The crowd whooped. Later, she found the alien studying security footage of humans dancing in the ration line.

“Your species,” Gloam rasped, “responds to benevolent authoritarianism with...”

“Relief,” Clara said softly. The medal chilled her palm. Somewhere beyond the towers, Luna was biking through pesticide-free meadows with other children who no longer hoarded Adderall to survive school.

The Zyrathi’s eyestalks drooped. Clara understood then—they’d expected resistance, not this terrible human talent for mistaking armistice for peace. She pocketed the medal, its alloy forged from melted-down credit card readers, and walked home through air that no longer tasted of burning.

input: Humanity is visited by a cosmic horror the likes of which has only been seen in Lovecraftian horror. In desperation, Earth throws everything we have at it, and, miraculously, the human race has killed a God. Somewhere in a realm beyond our understanding, the other gods speak of the event.
output:
They found Him in the garden where the oldest prayers wilted, His shadow still pooling like spilled ink beneath the fig trees. The others arrived one by one, their forms shimmering at the edges—a headache of light, a sigh of smoke.

“They gnawed through His spine with machines,” said He Who Parts the Veil, plucking a rotten pomegranate from a branch. His voice was the crackle of glaciers calving. “Primitive things. Cogs and sparks.”

She Who Holds the Vastness knelt, her fingertips brushing the god-corpses’s wrist. The flesh there had already petrified into a black, volcanic glass. “You’re certain it wasn’t… another of us?”

“They crowned it a war,” said the One Cloaked in Falling Teeth. His laughter was a swarm of locusts. “Humans. They name everything. Even their terrors.”

A wind stirred, carrying the stench of burnt ozone and something sweeter beneath—sweat, maybe, or adrenaline. The garden’s horizon flickered, its usual timeless twilight now threaded with a feverish, electric blue.

“They’ll expect retribution,” murmured She Who Holds the Vastness. Her many eyes reflected the corpse’s jagged angles. “We should flood their cities. Unmake their laws of physics.”

He Who Parts the Veil crushed the pomegranate. Seeds like teeth spilled. “And if they win again?”

Silence. The fig trees trembled, shedding centuries of unanswered prayers—cure her, bring him home, let me live, let me die.

The youngest of them materialized last, a thing of fraying starlight and static. It had no true name, only a sound like a radio dial spun too fast. “They mourned Him,” it buzzed. “After. They lit fires and sang.”

The others turned.

“I lingered,” it said. “In the ash. Their voices… they didn’t sound victorious. They sounded guilty. Like children who’d broken a beloved toy.”

“Guilt,” sneered the One Cloaked in Falling Teeth. “A parasite emotion. It changes nothing.”

“Doesn’t it?” The youngest’s light pulsed. “They wept because they’d won. Because they finally saw the wound they’d made in the dark.”

She Who Holds the Vastness stood, her silhouette warping into something jagged and avian. “You’re suggesting we let this stand? That we allow vermin to think they can—”

“They know,” interrupted the youngest. “That’s the trap. Now they’ll always wonder what else they can kill. What else is killable.”

Another silence. The corpse’s shadow had begun to crystallize, creeping across the garden floor in jagged lattices. Somewhere, a prayer from 312 A.D. dissolved into moths.

“We’ll quarantine them,” said He Who Parts the Veil finally. “Let their planet fester in isolation. No more visitations, no more revelations.”

“Too late,” murmured the youngest. “They’ll come looking now. They’ll invent new machines. New reasons.”

The garden dimmed. The fig trees, sensing discord, began to fold their leaves.

“Then what?” snapped the One Cloaked in Falling Teeth. “You want us to fear them?”

The youngest drifted toward the corpse, its light grazing the glassy flesh. “I want us to understand. They didn’t slay Him because they hated gods. They slew Him because they needed gods. Needed to prove they could exist without us.”

A tremor passed through the garden. The horizon’s electric blue deepened, bleeding into the black.

She Who Holds the Vastness tilted her head. “You sound almost… fond.”

The youngest dimmed. “I’ve been listening too long.”

They left the corpse there. Let it become a monument, or a mountain, or a myth. Let the garden grow around it, strangling and strange.

But later, when the others had dissolved back into their realms, the youngest returned. It hovered over the shadow, now a sprawling obsidian scar, and did something none of them had done in eons.

It whispered a prayer.

input: Instead of the Monkey’s Paw, you find the Clown’s Nose, which instead of granting your wish in the worst way possible will grant it in the funniest way.
output:
His avatar, Henry, wore overalls and a straw hat. Each morning, Henry stepped onto a pixelated porch, stretched, and yawned at a sunrise rendered in 8-bit gold. Elias would lean close, the monitor’s glow etching his gaunt face blue, and guide Henry through chores—tilling soil, milking cows, tossing feed to chickens that clucked in tinny MIDI. At noon, Henry napped under an oak tree while light dappled his overalls. Elias never skipped this part. He’d watch the screen until his eyes burned, imagining warmth on his neck.Martin found the nose in the breast pocket of suit #4—charcoal wool, double-vented, still warm from the dryer. The deceased had been a circus clown. "Natural causes," the file said, though Martin noted the man’s smile lines had outlived his actual smile by decades. The nose was cherry-red, rubbery, faintly sticky. He pressed it to his own face on a whim.

Click.

A sound like a whoopee cushion deflating. Then silence.

That night, in the embalming room’s antiseptic hush, Martin muttered, "Wouldn’t mind some company." His voice startled him. Thirty-seven, divorced, speaking to clown paraphernalia. The fluorescent lights buzzed.

The next morning, a troupe of unicyclists circled the chapel parking lot.

"Birthday party for a Mr. Albert Gunderson?" their leader asked, rainbow suspenders straining.

"There’s been a—" Martin began, but a minivan disgorged eight children clutching Goodwill tutus. A terrier in a cone-collar herded them inside.

The viewing for Mrs. Eleanor Riggs became a hybrid affair. Mourners in black sniffled beside toddlers hyped on Sprite. A girl in dinosaur pajamas left Cheez-It offerings at the casket. The terrier peed on Martin’s Oxfords.

"Chaos," he hissed later, scrubbing the leather.

Chaos, his ex-wife used to say, is just order you’re not brave enough to dance with. She’d twirled through their apartment in mismatched socks, trailing cinnamon and Leonard Cohen lyrics. Martin had measured coffee grounds level to the teaspoon.

By Thursday, three more "parties" arrived. A Quinceañera. A D&D group. A man claiming to be an amateur tightrope walker ("I just need height, man"). Each time, Martin’s protestations dissolved when children’s laughter ricocheted off the marble angels, when the D&D teens shyly asked about his work, when the tightrope enthusiast wept over his dead cat.

The nose glowed in his desk drawer.

On Saturday, a woman with peacock hair brought a ukulele. "Funeral for my brother," she said, eyeing the clown nose now perched on Martin’s clipboard. "He loved pratfalls. Once mailed himself to Fiji as a bit."

Martin adjusted his tie. "We usually recommend—"

"Play something sad," she interrupted. "But make it swing."

He strummed. She tap-danced. The mourners—half strangers from prior parties—swayed. Someone spilled Merlot on the Persian rug. Someone else laughed, high and startled, and Martin felt something in his chest uncrimp.

Later, alone with the nose, he pressed it to his face.

Click.

Nothing changed.

He laughed anyway—raw, creaky, like a porch swing needing oil. The refrigerators hummed along.

In the morning, he placed the nose in suit #4’s pocket before sealing the casket. The clown’s makeup looked less waxy now, almost mischievous. Outside, a juggler practiced with lacquered skulls from the display shelf.

"Not a permanent addition," Martin warned, but he held the door open wider.

Chaos, he was learning, had its own liturgy. You didn’t control it; you let it slip its hand into yours, sweaty and trusting, and followed where it led.
